## Status and purpose

### Interpreting support rather than just a winner

The fit's `assignments` table now includes `PROBABILITY_MARGIN` (largest minus
second-largest membership probability), `NORMALIZED_ENTROPY` (zero for a
concentrated assignment, one for uniform probabilities), and `ASSIGNMENT_STATUS`.
No universal confidence cutoff is imposed. These quantities are conditional on
the fitted model and K, not calibrated probabilities that a biological assignment
is correct. No-information samples and exact ties remain unassigned; an unfinished
fit is explicitly labelled. For K = 1, margin and entropy are undefined (`NA`):
probability one is not evidence of panmixia.

`start.diagnostics` reports label-invariant `PARTITION_ARI_VS_SELECTED` and
`N_COMPARABLE`, alongside objective gaps and convergence. Only informative,
positive-weight training samples with untied assignments are compared. An ARI of
one means identical partitions, not correct populations. Inspect failed and
unfinished starts separately. If compact partition storage exceeds
`max.genotypes`, `start.partition.assessment` says not assessed, and comparison
values are `NA`. No matrices of all starts' allele frequencies are retained.

The CV result adds `fold.support`, per-K `GAP_FROM_BEST` in `summary`, and
`support.flags`. Fold ties are retained rather than counted as decisive wins.
Flags identify incomplete comparisons, disagreeing/tied fold winners, a winner
at the upper grid boundary, and recorded fitting warnings. Shared training data
make folds dependent: votes and score gaps are descriptive, not confidence
intervals, significance tests or posterior probabilities of K. A K = 1 winner
means no supported split under this fitted comparison, not proven panmixia.
No flags does not certify reliable structure. Assignment agreement across CV
refits is not currently calculated; fold support concerns predictive K only.

See `inst/experimental/stock-mixture-evidence-review.md` for the consolidated
simulation findings and unresolved validation requirements for Scott's review.

**Research prototype: not yet a validated stock-delineation workflow.**
The functions below are internal, unexported development interfaces. Their names
and results may change. Scott Foster's methodological and code review is required
before release. In particular, successful numerical tests do not establish
confidence-interval coverage or reliable estimation of the number of stocks.

This model extends the discrete-mixture idea discussed by Foster and colleagues
to uncertain genotypes. It is separate from `assign_likelihood_dapc()`: there is
no discriminant training step and no supplied population labels in fitting.
It is also **not an admixture model**. An individual belongs to one latent
component; its membership probabilities express uncertainty about that component,
not fractions of its genome inherited from different ancestral populations.

Genetic clusters alone do not establish demographically independent management
stocks. Sampling design, movement, reproduction, temporal stability and ecological
evidence remain necessary for a management interpretation.

## Data contract and preparation

Supply an existing SeqArray Genomic Data Structure (GDS) file or open handle.
Only active samples and variants are analysed. Borrowed handles and filters are
restored, and the input file is not modified. Genotypes must be diploid and
biallelic, with likelihoods ordered REF/REF, REF/ALT, ALT/ALT.

| Field | Meaning | Treatment |
|:--|:--|:--|
| GL | Log10 genotype likelihood | Converted to natural logs |
| PL | Nonnegative integer Phred likelihood | Converted to natural logs |
| GP | Genotype posterior probability | Not accepted as a likelihood substitute |
| GT | Hard genotype call | No automatic fallback |
| Fully missing or flat vector | No genotype evidence | Neutral in the likelihood |
| Partly missing vector | Incomplete likelihood record | Rejected |

Automatic selection prefers PL, then GL; specify the field explicitly when both
exist. Having three values does not prove the variant caller used an appropriate
diploid model. Check calling settings, reference/ALT coding and retained fields.

Filter mapping/calling artefacts, inspect missingness by sample, population and
batch, and address close relatives and linkage disequilibrium before interpreting
structure. GL/PL accounts for genotype uncertainty, **not** biased mapping,
allele dropout or incorrect likelihood calibration. Sparse non-model datasets
can cluster by technical quality rather than biology.

Optional metadata uses `INDIVIDUALS` and, when available, `STRATA`. Metadata is
matched by ID and returned for auditing, not used as known component labels.
Sampling strata and inferred components need not correspond.

## Model and computation

For individual \(i\), marker \(l\), stock \(k\), genotype \(g\), ALT frequency
\(p_{lk}\), mixture proportion \(\pi_k\), and likelihood \(L_{ilg}\),

\[
\ell = \sum_i w_i \log\left[
  \sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\prod_l\sum_{g=0}^2
  L_{ilg}{2\choose g}p_{lk}^{g}(1-p_{lk})^{2-g}
\right].
\]

The Hardy--Weinberg genotype prior is conditional on stock. Markers are treated
as independent conditional on stock. Strong linkage can therefore exaggerate
membership certainty; streaming more markers does not resolve that assumption.

Expectation--maximization (EM) integrates genotype uncertainty and updates
frequencies and proportions. Missing observations do not contribute fabricated
allele counts. Samples with no informative likelihoods receive the mixture prior
and an `NA` assignment. All-uninformative markers cause an explicit error.

Likelihoods are streamed in blocks. Memory still includes marker-by-stock
frequencies and sample-by-stock memberships: `max.genotypes` limits one block,
not total memory. Smaller blocks reduce memory but increase reading overhead.

The first start uses supplied frequencies. By default subsequent starts use
random soft partitions; the opt-in mixed strategy is described below. The
highest-objective converged start is selected. With no regularization the
objective equals the data log likelihood. Inspect
`start.diagnostics`: convergence is not proof of a global optimum, and random
starts may miss small groups. Component labels are arbitrary.

## Fit a specified K

This example assumes a prepared file; it is not run during vignette building.
Starting frequencies require **GDS variant IDs**, not VCF annotation IDs.

```{r fit, eval=FALSE}
gds <- SeqArray::seqOpen("likelihoods.gds", readonly = TRUE)
ids <- SeqArray::seqGetData(gds, "variant.id")
initial <- matrix(0.5, length(ids), 3,
                  dimnames = list(as.character(ids), paste0("STOCK_", 1:3)))
fit <- assigner:::.sm_fit_gds(
  gds, frequency = initial, likelihood = "PL",
  n.starts = 13, start.strategy = "mixed", init.max.snps = 1000,
  seed = 2026, block.snps = 500
)
fit$start.diagnostics
fit$proportion
fit$membership
fit$frequency.estimable
fit$likelihood.information.audit
SeqArray::seqClose(gds)
```

Identical starting columns cannot split by themselves; this example needs the
additional starts. Thirteen starts is illustrative, not a validated sufficient
number. Repeat with independent seeds and compare likelihoods and partitions.

`frequency.support` is the membership-weighted count of informative individuals
per stock and marker, not sequencing depth. Unsupported frequencies are optimizer
placeholders, not estimates. Even a positive count may be too small for reliable
inference. Mixture proportions describe this sampling panel, not population size.

### Diverse starting points

`start.strategy = "mixed"` cycles through PCA/k-means starts using 2, 5 and 10
axes (limited by rank), a random soft partition, a split of a fitted K-1
component, and a perturbation of the best frequencies. The first supplied
start plus one cycle requires seven starts. Subsequent split starts cycle
through the lower-K components. A lower-K seed itself uses five random starts.
Failed starts and nonconvergence remain visible in `start.diagnostics`.

PCA uses at most `init.max.snps` evenly spaced active markers and only positive
weight, informative training individuals. The matrix is also capped by
`max.genotypes`, although SVD adds workspace. Missing likelihoods are temporarily
represented by pooled expected dosages for this initialization only. These
values never replace likelihoods in EM or modify the GDS. Repeated k-means
initialization is not simulated annealing, and none of these choices guarantees
that PCA has removed missingness or batch effects. Compare inferred memberships
with call rate, depth and technical metadata.

`likelihood.information.audit` reports component-weighted uninformative fractions and
training-sample membership correlations with those fractions. Flat likelihoods
count as uninformative even when a genotype record exists. Correlations are
unweighted across unique informative training individuals, and are `NA` when
either variable is constant. An association merits investigation, not automatic
sample removal. `near.best.starts` counts converged starts within the relative
objective tolerance of the selected fit; it is not a global-optimum certificate.

### Regularized prediction

`epsilon` bounds frequencies away from zero and one. It is not a sequencing
error estimate or a fitted prior. A small component may lack a rare allele in
training yet contain it in new samples; the bound then strongly affects prediction.
Do not choose it simply to obtain a preferred K.

Two optional regularizers are available, leaving `regularization = "none"` as
the unchanged default. `"symmetric"` fixes the center q to 0.5; `"pooled"`
estimates a separate q per marker from training likelihoods alone. A positive
`prior.strength = s` specifies Beta(1+s*q, 1+s*(1-q)) priors. The fitted objective
is the data log likelihood plus

\[
s\sum_{l,k}\{q_l\log p_{lk}+(1-q_l)\log(1-p_{lk})\}.
\]

The M step adds s*q pseudo-ALT counts and s total pseudo-allele counts to the
expected counts. This is a bounded maximum-a-posteriori update, **not** a
posterior mean or integration over frequency uncertainty. Pooled centers stay
fixed during each fit, and are re-estimated from the relevant training or
bootstrap individuals. This is not a fully fitted hierarchical model.

```{r regularized, eval=FALSE}
fit_regularized <- assigner:::.sm_fit_gds(
  "likelihoods.gds", initial, start.strategy = "mixed", n.starts = 13,
  regularization = "pooled", prior.strength = 2, seed = 2026
)
fit_regularized$objective.history  # penalized objective should increase
fit_regularized$history            # data likelihood alone need not increase
```

The value 2 is an illustrative fixed candidate, not an established default or
optimal setting. Excessive shrinkage can obscure private alleles and weak
structure. Any tuning needs training-only inner validation and an untouched
outer evaluation. Held-out scores exclude the prior penalty. Do not compare
penalized objectives across different K or prior settings. Unsupported
stock-marker frequencies may be prior-driven and remain flagged as unsupported.

The strength matters most for small groups. With four fully informative
diploid training individuals, s = 2 contributes 2/(8+2), or 20%, of the
frequency update's total allele-count weight. With two individuals it contributes
one third. These are pseudo-counts, not extra genotypes or independent evidence.
The effective count can be fractional when stock membership is uncertain.

## Fixed-K uncertainty

```{r bootstrap, eval=FALSE}
uncertainty <- assigner:::.sm_bootstrap_gds(
  "likelihoods.gds", fit, B = 200, seed = 2026,
  n.starts = 3, frequency.variants = character()
)
uncertainty$diagnostics
uncertainty$intervals
```

This is an ordinary whole-individual bootstrap, **not stockR's Bayesian
bootstrap**. Refit components are aligned to reference frequencies before
percentile intervals are formed. Alignment currently supports K at most 12.
It can be ambiguous when components merge or overlap. Individuals are assumed
independent; relatedness and repeated samples need a different resampling design.

Intervals condition on K and the selected marker panel. They do not include
uncertainty about K, ascertainment, or unobserved alleles. Whole-individual
resampling preserves linked marker vectors but does not correct the model's
independence assumption. Coverage under realistic low-depth data remains untested.
Any unusable replicate withholds the interval summary; inspect failures rather
than silently discarding them. Selected frequency intervals require supported
cells. `max.values` limits retained bootstrap arrays.

## Held-out comparison of K

```{r comparison, eval=FALSE}
# A named fold vector must be supplied from the sampling design.
# Keep relatives, repeated samples and other dependent units together.
comparison <- assigner:::.sm_cv_gds(
  "likelihoods.gds", K = 1:4, folds = folds_by_sample_id,
  n.starts = 13, seed = 2026, likelihood = "PL", start.strategy = "mixed",
  regularization = "pooled", prior.strength = 2
)
comparison$summary
comparison$diagnostics
```

Each fold estimates parameters from training individuals only and scores the
held-out individual's marginal mixture likelihood, not its best component.
The grid must include K = 1. All comparisons must use the same observations.
Incomplete comparisons return no preferred K. A winner at the upper grid boundary
does not demonstrate that larger K would be worse.

**Best predictive K is not a biological stock count.** The bundled stockR
simulation has three generating groups. Matched initialization recovers its
partition, but the initial 300-marker held-out comparison preferred K = 1 with
the default frequency bound and K = 2 with larger bounds. Consequently, automatic
stock-count selection is not validated. The reproducible investigation and
results are retained under `inst/experimental/`; this failure is not hidden by
the passing unit tests.

A follow-up separated optimization from prediction. The generating groups
contain 60, 6 and 34 individuals. Ten random starts missed the exact training
partition; training-only PCA initialization improved likelihood but also missed
it. Diagnostic initialization using the known training labels recovered it,
yet K = 3 still did not win held-out prediction. In the smallest group, each
fold has only four training individuals; 26–33 of the 300 markers contain an
allele seen in that group's held-out samples but absent in training. Better
initialization alone therefore does not resolve this benchmark. Those historical
results predate the mixed strategy and regularization extensions described here.
Oracle labels remain diagnostic only and are never used by the fitting interface.

## Validation and remaining limitations

A larger clean-data proof of concept used fresh population-frequency realizations,
300 training and 300 independent test individuals, and 1,000–10,000 markers.
With pooled strength fixed at 100 from an earlier pilot, predictive selection
recovered the generating K = 3 at drift approximately 0.005 in one of three
1,000-marker realizations and two of three at each larger marker count. Panels
were nested, not independent replicates across marker counts. Native stockR
Kmeans.EM fits evaluated by their returned AIC/BIC did not select K = 3 in those
panels, although supplying K = 3 gave perfect native test recovery at 5,000 and
10,000 markers. Both fresh null controls selected K = 1; both controls near
FST 0.001 remained unresolved. These small experiments support the regularized
workflow as a proof of concept, not a universal marker threshold, recommended
default strength or advantage of GL encoding itself. They use near-certain GLs
and different selection criteria. Full settings, failures and diagnostics are
recorded in `inst/experimental/stock-proof-fresh.md`.

A subsequent controlled experiment held 3,000 markers and initialization fixed
while increasing training samples from 100 to 200 to 300 fish per population.
Across three fresh frequency realizations, both fixed-strength and strength-tuned
predictive selection recovered K = 3 at each sample size; mean test ARI increased
from approximately 0.93–0.94 to 0.99 and 1.00. Tuning selected strength 200 and
improved predictive log scores, but did not improve hard classification at the
smallest sample size. All nested null panels retained K = 1. A separate post-hoc
revisit of an earlier missed realization recovered K = 3 with strength 500;
that value was at the grid boundary and is not a recommended default. Joint
strength/K selection here is an experimental benchmark workflow, not an added
public argument. See `inst/experimental/strength-size-experiment.md` for the
design, native stockR comparisons and qualifications.

In the first independent pilot (60 markers, two simulation seeds per scenario),
pooled strength 2 selected K=3 for balanced, unbalanced, low-depth and
population-structured-missingness three-group simulations. The K=1 and K=2
controls selected their generating K. Weak differentiation selected K=1, and
the original stockR example still selected K=2 rather than K=3. A separate
one-population missingness-only control selected K=1. These are small pilot
results, not estimated success rates or proof of robustness. Full numerical
outputs and reproducible scripts are retained in `inst/experimental/`.
Repeating the seven designs with 180 markers gave the same regularized winners
for both seeds. Across 60 and 180 markers, all 448 selected fits converged;
some individual starts failed and were reported. More markers alone did not
resolve the unregularized predictor's difficulty with small groups.

The 5,000-marker, 100-individual stockR example tests the near-certain genotype
limit. Matching that example does not validate uncertain low-coverage GL/PL.
Required further work includes replicated simulations across depth, missingness,
weak differentiation, unequal group sizes, LD and relatives; interval coverage;
initialization sensitivity; and predictive calibration of the new regularizers.
Model violations such as admixture, inbreeding or technical batches may produce
apparently strong but misleading components.

Retain the source commit, package versions, likelihood field, active sample and
marker IDs, QC choices, seeds, starts, folds, frequency bounds and convergence
diagnostics. No default removes the need to examine the biological sampling design.
